meta.title: Reading the Fretboard
meta.summary: Six strings, one rule, and the two places the alphabet skips a step.

spans.text: A fretboard looks like a hundred and thirty separate notes to memorise. It is really
— and once you know where the repeats are, the neck stops being a map you memorise and becomes one you can read.

: the smallest distance Western music uses. Move up one fret and the note rises by that much. Move up twelve and you are back where you started, an octave higher. That is the whole system — everything after this is bookkeeping.
The bookkeeping starts with the open strings. In standard tuning, counting the thinnest string as string 1:
A B C D E F G
and then start over. Between most neighbouring letters sits a sharp — a fret you skip over when you say the letters out loud. Between two pairs there is nothing at all:
Those two gaps cause nearly every early fretboard mistake. Count frets expecting a sharp between B and C and every note above it lands one fret too high.
Counting up from the open fifth string, then, string 5 reads
A A# B C C# D D# E F F# G G#
The dots are doing you a favour
Inlays are not decoration. Frets 3, 5, 7 and 9 are marked, and the double dot at fret 12 is the octave — the open string's note again, halfway up the neck. Learn the marked frets on the two
strings first, and you can reach any other note by counting one or two frets from an anchor you already know.

. The seventh fret is a reliable place to find a chord's fifth.

string. Above it, the whole neck repeats.

Name notes out loud while you play them. It feels slow and slightly ridiculous for about a week, and then the neck is simply legible.
